title: What's Your Focused Finish?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Building on his 'Limping vs. Striving' framing from the prior week, Dave Stuart Jr. lays out the practical mechanics of choosing a Focused Finish for the final quarter of the school year. He argues that teachers who end the year feeling strongest don't try to accomplish everything on their list, but instead strategically direct limited energy toward one to three chosen areas. His method is a simple two-step process: pick a category using whatever framework already makes sense to you (his own Five Key Beliefs, the competency areas in The Will to Learn, or the six things in These 6 Things), then commit to one to three SMART-ish goals or experiments inside that category. He illustrates the approach with his own past examples (weekly Pop-Up Debates, daily provisional writing) and current ones (Woodenizing AI use, a round of MGC check-ins), plus examples from a colleague named Caleb who is focusing on mini-sermons and weekly feedback. He closes by inviting readers to answer two reflection questions and clarifies that choosing a Focused Finish doesn't mean neglecting the rest of one's practice — it means being intentional about where the best energy goes.
points: Teachers who finish the year with the greatest sense of strength don't chase every goal at 100% — they strategically concentrate limited energy on one to three chosen areas, a pattern Stuart calls counterintuitive but dependable.
The Focused Finish process is reduced to two deliberately simple steps: pick a category using a framework you already trust, then commit to one to three SMART-ish goals inside it.

Concrete past examples (weekly Pop-Up Debates culminating in Pop-Up Toasts, daily provisional writing tracked by word count) show the Focused Finish idea translated into specific, repeatable classroom routines rather than abstract intentions.
A colleague's parallel examples (twice-weekly written mini-sermons, weekly specific feedback, a more regular MGC cadence) demonstrate that the same framework adapts to different teachers' priorities.
Stuart explicitly reframes a Focused Finish as additive, not substitutive — it doesn't excuse neglecting the rest of one's practice, it just directs the best energy toward one chosen area.
quotes: Those who finish the year with the greatest sense of strength in their soul don't try to reach every possible goal and complete every possible thing at 100%. Rather, they strategically direct their energy.
My mind is too simple for most evaluation rubrics; when I read them, all I see is an overcomplicated word salad.
Complete one Pop-Up Debate per week between now and year's end, culminating in Pop-Up Toasts on the last day.
Woodenizing the effective use of AI to support (rather than misguidedly replace) the work of learning.
If you had to pick one area of your teaching practice to improve between now and year's end, what would you pick?
Remember that identifying some Focused Finish work doesn't mean neglecting everything else. We still maintain a sustainable status quo in the other areas of our practice.
